# Multiple endocrine neoplasia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Multiple endocrine neoplasia > Multiple endocrine neoplasia*

[Original Article Link](/library/hg0cE2)

---

## Summary

Multiple endocrine <u>neoplasia</u> (MEN) is a term used to describe three <u>autosomal dominant</u> syndromes that are associated with certain <u>hormone</u>-producing neoplasias. There are three subtypes: <u>MEN 1</u>, <u>MEN 2A</u>, and <u>MEN 2B</u>. <u>MEN 1</u> is caused by an altered <u>menin protein</u> expression and presents with <u>primary hyperparathyroidism</u>, often in association with endocrine <u>pancreatic</u> tumors and/or <u>pituitary adenomas</u>. <u>MEN 2A</u> and <u>MEN 2B</u> are caused by a mutated <u>RET</u> <u>proto-oncogene</u> and both present with <u>medullary thyroid carcinoma</u> and sometimes <u>pheochromocytoma</u>. <u>MEN 2A</u> is further associated with <u>primary hyperparathyroidism</u> as well, while <u>MEN 2B</u> causes a <u>marfanoid habitus</u> and sometimes <u>neurinomas</u>. If any of the individual conditions associated with MEN are suspected, especially in patients with a positive <u>family history</u>, it is important to consider a diagnostic workup for any of the other associations. Specific diagnostic and management approaches can be found within the articles for each of the individual conditions. Family members of MEN patients should receive <u>genetic counseling</u>. Those positive for mutated <u>genes</u> should be closely monitored and should undergo a <u>total thyroidectomy</u> if positive for the <u>RET</u> <u>proto-oncogene</u>.

---

## Overview

| Overview of multiple endocrine neoplasia |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Feature | <br>MEN 1 (formerly known as <u>Wermer syndrome</u>) | MEN 2 |  |
| <br>MEN 2A (formerly known as <u>Sipple syndrome</u>) | MEN 2B |  |  |
| Genetics | <br>* Mutation of the <u>MEN1</u> <u>gene</u> (located on <u>chromosome</u> 11) → altered expression of menin protein<br><br> | <br>* Altered expression of the <u>RET proto-oncogene</u> → elevated <u>tyrosine kinase</u> activity<br><br> |  |
| Inheritance | <br>* <u>Autosomal dominant</u><br><br> |  |  |
| Principal manifestations | <br>* <u>Primary hyperparathyroidism</u> (<u>parathyroid adenoma</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Medullary thyroid carcinoma</u><br><br> |  |
| Further manifestations | <br><br>* Endocrine <u>pancreatic</u> tumors <br><br>* <u>Gastrinoma</u> (most common)<br><br>* <u>Insulinoma</u><br><br>* <u>VIPoma</u><br><br>* <u>Glucagonoma</u> (rare)<br><br>* <u>Pituitary adenoma</u>: most commonly <u>prolactinoma</u><br><br>* <u>Neuroendocrine tumors</u> (∼ 10–15% of cases)<br><br>* Nonendocrine tumors (e.g. <u>angiofibromas</u>, collagenomas, <u>meningiomas</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Pheochromocytoma</u> (∼ 40% of cases) [[1]](/library/Oj0I0T)<br><br> |  |
| <br>* <u>Primary hyperparathyroidism</u> (∼ 20–30% of cases)[[2]](/library/lj0v0T)<br><br> | <br><br>* Multiple neurinomas: mucosal neuromas (e.g., <u>lips</u>, <u>tongue</u>), intestinal ganglioneuromatosis )  [[3]](/library/Nj0-0T)<br><br>* Marfanoid habitus<br><br><br> |  |  |
| Management | <br><br>* <u>Parathyroidectomy</u><br><br>* Excision of <u>pancreatic</u> <u>tumor</u><br><br>* Transsphenoidal <u>surgery</u> for excision of <u>pituitary adenoma</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Thyroidectomy</u> including cervical <u>lymph nodes</u><br>* <u>Pheochromocytoma</u> should first be ruled out (e.g., by measuring urine <u>metanephrines</u>) or treated before undergoing <u>surgery</u><br><br>* If <u>pheochromocytoma</u>: <u>adrenalectomy</u><br><br>* If <u>hyperparathyroidism</u>: <u>parathyroidectomy</u><br><br><br> |  |





> [!NOTE]
> <u>MEN 1</u>: 3 "P"s = Parathyroid, Pancreas, Pituitary gland




> [!NOTE]
> <u>MEN 2A</u>: 1 "M", 2 "P”s = Medullary <u>thyroid carcinoma</u>, Pheochromocytoma, Parathyroid




> [!NOTE]
> <u>MEN 2B</u>: 2 “M”s, 1 “P” = Medullary <u>thyroid carcinoma</u>, Marfanoid habitus/Multiple <u>neuromas</u>, Pheochromocytoma




> [!NOTE]
> Remembering that the <u>inheritance pattern</u> of MEN syndromes is <u>autosomal</u> dominant requires MENtal dominance.
